title: Guanfacine and Alcohol: Dizziness, Fainting, and Safe Use
excerpt: Can you drink on guanfacine (Intuniv, Tenex)? How the two lower blood pressure and cause drowsiness together, the fainting and rebound risks, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Can you drink on guanfacine or Intuniv? How alcohol adds to its blood pressure drop and drowsiness, fainting and rebound risks, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** guanfacine and alcohol push your body in the same direction. Guanfacine (sold as Intuniv for ADHD and as Tenex, or generic guanfacine, for blood pressure) lowers your blood pressure, slows your heart rate, and makes many people sleepy. Alcohol widens blood vessels, lowers blood pressure for several hours after you drink, dehydrates you, and is a sedative. Put them together and the most likely problems are dizziness, lightheadedness when you stand up, heavy drowsiness, and in some people fainting. The prescribing information for extended-release guanfacine advises patients to avoid alcohol, and that is the safest default. If you do drink, the risk is mostly about how much, how fast, and what happens afterward, especially if a hangover makes you skip or throw up your dose.

**The quick rules:** Don't drink until you know how guanfacine affects you on its own. If your doctor is fine with occasional drinking, stick to the amount they approve, eat first, drink water, and sit or lie down at the first sign of lightheadedness. Stand up slowly. Never drive after combining the two. And never stop guanfacine suddenly because you plan to drink or because you feel rough the next day. Stopping abruptly can cause a sharp rebound rise in blood pressure.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor before drinking on guanfacine if** you've recently started it or changed your dose, you take it for high blood pressure, you have a heart condition or a slow heart rate, you've ever fainted, or you also take other sedating medicines such as sleep aids, anxiety medicines, opioids, or antihistamines. **Call 911 or go to the emergency room if** someone on guanfacine who has been drinking faints and doesn't come round quickly, is very hard to wake, has a very slow pulse, chest pain, trouble breathing, or confusion that doesn't clear.

## How Guanfacine and Alcohol Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

Guanfacine belongs to a group of medicines called **alpha-2A adrenergic agonists**. In plain terms, it turns down the volume on your body's "fight or flight" system. It acts on receptors in the brain that control how much adrenaline-like signaling goes out to your blood vessels and heart. Less of that signal means your blood vessels relax, your blood pressure drops, and your heart beats a little slower. In the front part of the brain, the same receptor type helps with attention and impulse control, which is why a version of the drug is used for ADHD.

Alcohol hits several of the same targets from a different angle:

1. **Blood pressure.** In the first hours after drinking, alcohol widens blood vessels, which tends to lower blood pressure. Guanfacine is already holding blood pressure down. The two effects add up, and the drop is most noticeable when you stand up quickly, because your body can't tighten blood vessels fast enough to keep blood flowing to your brain. That's the dizzy, gray-out feeling doctors call **orthostatic hypotension**, meaning a drop in blood pressure on standing.
2. **Heart rate.** Guanfacine can slow your pulse. Normally, when blood pressure falls, your heart speeds up to compensate. Guanfacine blunts that reflex, so you have less of a safety cushion when alcohol lowers your pressure.
3. **Sedation.** Sleepiness and fatigue are among the most common side effects of guanfacine, especially in the first weeks or after a dose increase. Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant, meaning it slows brain activity. Stacking them can leave you far drowsier and slower to react than either would on its own.
4. **Dehydration.** Alcohol makes you pee more, and a night of drinking often means losing fluid through sweating or vomiting too. Lower blood volume makes low blood pressure and fainting more likely.

There isn't a big body of research testing guanfacine and alcohol together in a controlled trial. The concern comes from how both substances work, from the drug's labeling, and from what clinicians see with similar blood pressure medicines. That's normal for this kind of interaction, and it's why the advice is cautious rather than precise.

### The rebound problem nobody mentions

The most underrated risk isn't the night out. It's the morning after. Guanfacine has to be taken every day, and stopping it suddenly can cause **rebound hypertension**, meaning your blood pressure climbs back up quickly and can overshoot where it started. People may also feel anxious, shaky, or have a racing heart and headache.

A heavy night can disrupt your dose in a few ways:

- You fall asleep without taking your evening dose.
- You vomit within a short time of taking it.
- You decide to "skip it" the next day because you feel awful or worry about mixing it with leftover alcohol.

One missed dose usually isn't a crisis, but missing two or more in a row is where the label warns of trouble. The extended-release label specifically tells prescribers to taper the drug, lowering the dose gradually, rather than stopping it abruptly. If you've missed doses, call your prescriber or pharmacist for advice on how to restart. Don't double up to catch up unless they tell you to.

## Intuniv and Alcohol vs. Tenex (Guanfacine IR) and Alcohol

Guanfacine comes in two main forms, and the difference matters a little for drinking.

| Form | Brand examples | Main use | What to know about alcohol |
|---|---|---|---|
| Extended-release (ER) | Intuniv, generic guanfacine ER | ADHD (approved for children and teens, often used off-label in adults) | Releases slowly over the day. Must be swallowed whole, never crushed or chewed. The label advises avoiding alcohol. |
| Immediate-release (IR) | Tenex (brand largely discontinued), generic guanfacine | High blood pressure; also used off-label for ADHD, tics, and sleep problems linked to PTSD | Usually taken at bedtime, so peak effects can overlap with a late night of drinking. |

**Intuniv and alcohol.** Because Intuniv is a slow-release tablet, its effect stays fairly steady through the day. You won't usually avoid the interaction by timing your drink, because the drug is in your system around the clock. Guanfacine has a long half-life, meaning it takes many hours for your body to clear half of a dose (often cited at around 17 hours in adults). Many people are prescribed Intuniv as young adults or college students, which is also when heavy drinking is common, so this combination comes up a lot.

**Guanfacine IR and alcohol.** Immediate-release tablets reach peak levels within a few hours. When it's taken at bedtime, which is common because it can make people sleepy, the peak can land right as you get home from a night out. That's a setup for a fall on the way to the bathroom at 3 a.m.

Whichever version you take, the advice is the same: alcohol adds to guanfacine's blood-pressure-lowering and sedating effects, and the safest choice is to avoid it or keep it to a small amount your doctor has approved.

## Can You Drink on Guanfacine at All?

This is the question most people actually want answered. The labeling for extended-release guanfacine advises avoiding alcohol, so the official answer leans toward no. In real life, some doctors are comfortable with an occasional drink for adults who have been on a stable dose for a while and have no problems with dizziness or low blood pressure. That decision belongs to you and your prescriber, not a website.

If your doctor says an occasional drink is okay, these habits lower the risk:

- **Wait until you're stable.** Avoid drinking for the first few weeks after starting guanfacine and after any dose change. That's when dizziness and drowsiness tend to be strongest.
- **Start very low.** Stay within the amount your doctor approved, drink it slowly, and see how you feel. Your usual tolerance may not apply on this medicine.
- **Eat first.** Food slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood, which softens the blood pressure dip.
- **Alternate with water.** Staying hydrated protects your blood volume, which helps your blood pressure.
- **Stand up slowly.** Sit on the edge of the bed or chair for a moment before standing, especially at night.
- **Don't drive.** Even modest drinking plus guanfacine can slow your reactions more than you'd expect.
- **Take your dose as usual** unless your doctor has told you otherwise. Skipping it to "make room" for alcohol trades one risk for another.

## Guanfacine and Alcohol Side Effects: What You Might Feel

The effects people report most often when mixing the two are exaggerated versions of guanfacine's usual side effects:

- **Dizziness or lightheadedness**, especially when getting up
- **Feeling faint**, tunnel vision, or "graying out"
- **Unusual drowsiness** or falling asleep earlier than expected
- **Slow, heavy feeling**, poor coordination, and slower reaction times
- **Dry mouth**, which guanfacine already causes and alcohol can worsen
- **Headache and fatigue** the next day

If you notice any of these, stop drinking, sit or lie down, drink some water, and don't drive. Most mild symptoms ease as the alcohol wears off. If someone gets worse rather than better, treat it as a medical problem.

## Guanfacine, Alcohol, and Fainting

Fainting, called **syncope**, is the most serious realistic risk for most people mixing these two. It's listed among the possible side effects of guanfacine even without alcohol, and the extended-release label warns about low blood pressure, slow heart rate, and fainting. Alcohol's blood-vessel-widening effect and dehydration make it more likely.

Why it happens: when you stand up, gravity pulls blood toward your legs. Normally your nervous system tightens blood vessels and nudges your heart rate up within seconds to keep blood flowing to your brain. Guanfacine dampens exactly that response, and alcohol relaxes the vessels further. If not enough blood reaches the brain for a few seconds, you pass out.

The faint itself is often brief, but the fall can cause head injuries, broken teeth, or worse. That's why the "stand up slowly" advice isn't a throwaway line.

**What to do if someone faints:**

- Lay them flat and, if they're not injured, raise their legs a little to help blood return to the brain.
- Check that they're breathing. If they're not breathing normally, call 911.
- Once they come round, keep them lying or sitting for a while and give water if they can swallow safely.
- If they've been drinking a lot, place them on their side so they won't choke if they vomit.

**Call 911** if they don't wake within a minute or so, they hit their head hard, they have chest pain or a very slow or irregular pulse, they're confused for more than a few minutes, or they faint more than once.

## Guanfacine Hangover: The Morning After

A hangover on guanfacine can feel worse than usual. You may wake up more tired and foggy, because both substances cause sedation and alcohol fragments your sleep. Dehydration from drinking can make the morning dizziness from guanfacine more noticeable.

Some practical steps:

- **Rehydrate before you get up properly.** A glass of water or an oral rehydration drink on the bedside table helps.
- **Get up in stages.** Sit up, wait, then stand. Morning is a common time for dizzy spells.
- **Take your usual dose** unless you were told otherwise. If you vomited your dose or aren't sure whether you took it, call a pharmacist rather than guessing.
- **Be careful with hangover medicines.** Sedating antihistamines found in "PM" products and some nausea medicines can add to drowsiness. Ask a pharmacist before combining anything with guanfacine.
- **Eat something simple.** It helps steady your blood sugar and settle your stomach.

If your heart is pounding, you have a severe headache, or you feel jittery the day after a night when you missed doses, that could be rebound from missed guanfacine rather than a normal hangover. Contact your prescriber. Our guide to [a racing heart after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) covers the common causes and when that symptom needs attention.

## How Long After Taking Guanfacine Can You Drink?

There is no safe waiting window to aim for. Because guanfacine is taken daily and has a long half-life, there's always a meaningful amount in your system. Waiting a few hours after your dose doesn't clear it, and skipping a dose to drink is a bad trade because of the rebound risk.

If you're on immediate-release guanfacine at bedtime, some people find it helps to finish any drinking well before their dose time so the alcohol peak and the drug peak don't land together. That's a sensible general idea, not a guarantee, and it's worth running past your prescriber. For extended-release forms like Intuniv, timing makes much less difference.

## Guanfacine and Alcohol for ADHD: Extra Things to Know

Many people taking guanfacine for ADHD also take a stimulant such as Adderall, Vyvanse, or Ritalin, since guanfacine is often added on. Alcohol interacts differently with each, and the combination of a stimulant, guanfacine, and alcohol gets complicated: the stimulant can mask how drunk you feel, while guanfacine and alcohol pull blood pressure and alertness down. Our overview of [ADHD medication and alcohol](/never-hungover/adhd-medication-and-alcohol) explains how the main ADHD drugs differ. If you've been switched between non-stimulants, our guide to [Strattera and alcohol](/never-hungover/strattera-and-alcohol) covers the other common option.

It's also worth knowing that ADHD and drinking problems overlap more than many people realize. If you notice you drink more than you mean to, that's worth mentioning to your prescriber. It's a normal part of an ADHD medication check-in, not a confession.

## Guanfacine and Alcohol for Blood Pressure

If you take guanfacine for high blood pressure, two things pull in opposite directions. In the short term, a few drinks lower your blood pressure and can stack with guanfacine to make you dizzy. Over the longer term, regular heavy drinking *raises* blood pressure and can make blood pressure medicines work less well. So frequent drinking can undo the reason you're taking the drug, while a single heavy night can push your pressure too low.

The blood pressure picture after drinking is surprisingly complex, including the rebound rise many people get the next day. Our guide to [high blood pressure after drinking](/never-hungover/high-blood-pressure-after-drinking) explains the pattern. If you take more than one blood pressure medicine, the combination with alcohol is stronger again. Beta blockers, for example, also slow the heart; see [propranolol and alcohol](/never-hungover/propranolol-and-alcohol) for how that class compares.

## Other Interactions That Make Alcohol Riskier on Guanfacine

Alcohol is rarely the only thing in the mix. These can make the combination more intense:

- **Other sedatives:** sleep aids, benzodiazepines, opioid painkillers, muscle relaxants, and sedating antihistamines all add to drowsiness.
- **Other blood pressure medicines:** more blood pressure lowering means more dizziness and fainting risk.
- **Medicines and foods that affect CYP3A4:** guanfacine is broken down mainly by a liver enzyme called CYP3A4. Some antifungals, certain antibiotics, and grapefruit juice can slow that breakdown and raise guanfacine levels. Some seizure medicines and St. John's wort can speed it up and lower levels. Ask a pharmacist to check your list.
- **High-fat meals with extended-release guanfacine:** the label notes that a high-fat meal raises how much of the drug your body absorbs, so ER guanfacine shouldn't be taken with one. A greasy late-night meal after drinking is worth keeping in mind.

For a broader look at how common medicines interact with supplements and alcohol, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You're at higher risk from mixing guanfacine and alcohol if you:

- Recently started guanfacine or had a dose increase
- Take it for high blood pressure alongside other blood pressure medicines
- Have a slow heart rate, heart rhythm problems, or a history of fainting
- Tend to get dizzy when you stand up, even without alcohol
- Take other sedating medicines
- Are older, since falls and low blood pressure are more dangerous with age
- Are under the legal drinking age, which is a separate issue but matters because Intuniv is commonly prescribed to teens

If any of these describe you, talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking at all.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

Some people who drink occasionally look for supplements to make the next day easier. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and on how alcohol acts in the brain. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data. There is no good evidence that DHM changes how guanfacine and alcohol interact, and it won't protect you from low blood pressure, drowsiness, or fainting. DHM's own interactions with prescription drugs haven't been well studied, so ask your doctor or pharmacist before adding it if you take guanfacine.

If your doctor is fine with it and you want to try DHM on the occasional night you drink, a well-reviewed option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) is a popular premium choice. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains timing and amounts, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. The habits in our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover), mainly drinking less, eating, and hydrating, matter far more than any supplement, especially on a medicine that lowers blood pressure.

## The Bottom Line

- Guanfacine and alcohol both lower blood pressure and both cause drowsiness. Together they can cause dizziness, heavy sedation, and fainting.
- The extended-release (Intuniv) label advises avoiding alcohol. If your doctor allows an occasional drink, keep it small, eat, hydrate, stand up slowly, and don't drive.
- Timing your drink around your dose doesn't make much difference, because guanfacine stays in your system all day.
- Never stop guanfacine suddenly to drink or because of a hangover. Missing doses can cause rebound high blood pressure.
- Fainting that doesn't resolve quickly, a very slow pulse, chest pain, or someone who is hard to wake are reasons to call 911.

Guanfacine is also one of several medicines that lower blood pressure. Our [blood pressure medication and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/blood-pressure-medication-and-alcohol) compares how the main types interact with drinking.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking guanfacine?**

The prescribing information for extended-release guanfacine advises avoiding alcohol, so the safest answer is no. Both lower blood pressure and cause drowsiness, and together they can cause dizziness and fainting. Some doctors allow an occasional drink for adults on a stable dose without side effects. Ask your prescriber what's right for you, and if you do drink, keep it to a small amount with food and water.

**What happens if you mix Intuniv and alcohol?**

Intuniv is extended-release guanfacine. Mixing it with alcohol can make you much sleepier than usual and can drop your blood pressure, causing lightheadedness, especially when you stand up, and sometimes fainting. Because Intuniv releases slowly and lasts all day, timing your drinks around the dose doesn't avoid the interaction. Don't drive after combining them.

**Can guanfacine and alcohol make you faint?**

Yes, it's possible. Guanfacine can cause low blood pressure, a slow heart rate, and fainting on its own, and alcohol widens blood vessels and dehydrates you. Together they make it harder for your body to keep blood flowing to your brain when you stand up. Stand up slowly, sit down at the first sign of lightheadedness, and call 911 if someone faints and doesn't wake quickly or hits their head.

**Should I skip my guanfacine dose if I'm going to drink?**

No, not without your doctor's advice. Guanfacine is meant to be taken every day, and stopping suddenly or missing several doses can cause rebound high blood pressure, along with anxiety, a racing heart, and headache. If you've missed doses after a night out, call your prescriber or pharmacist about how to restart rather than doubling up.

**How long after taking guanfacine can I drink alcohol?**

There isn't a waiting period that makes it safe. Guanfacine has a long half-life and is taken daily, so it's always in your system. For immediate-release guanfacine taken at bedtime, finishing any drinking well before your dose time may keep the peaks from overlapping, but that's a general idea to check with your prescriber, not a guarantee.

**Why do I feel so bad the day after drinking on guanfacine?**

Both guanfacine and alcohol cause sedation, and alcohol disrupts sleep and dehydrates you, so hangovers can feel heavier and dizzier than usual. If you also missed a dose, a pounding heart, headache, or jitteriness could be rebound from missed guanfacine. Rehydrate, get up slowly, take your normal dose unless told otherwise, and contact your prescriber if symptoms are strong.

**Is it safe to take DHM with guanfacine?**

DHM's interactions with prescription drugs haven't been well studied, and there is no good evidence that it reduces the guanfacine and alcohol interaction. It won't prevent low blood pressure, drowsiness, or fainting. Ask your doctor or pharmacist before combining DHM with guanfacine or any other daily medicine.
